messages.subject: How to determine goodness of fit?
parts:
As far as I know, AIC and BIC is for comparing several models, not for whether accepting a model. I can not make sure whether it's a good fit or not.
Did hypothesis testing like p-value or chi-squared test exist when using bayesian approach?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to determine goodness of fit?
parts:
There are lots of ways to evaluate the predictions of
models and to compare them, but we can't provide
a tutorial via e-mail. There are lots of resources
out there on Bayes. See, e.g., Gelman et al.'s
Bayesian Data Analysis book or the BUGS book. We
particularly like cross-validation-based measures, of
which WAIC is an approximation. And informal measures
like posterior predictive checking.

Yes, you can compute things like chi-squared tests and
also look at posterior intervals if you want.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to determine goodness of fit?
parts:
> On Jan 7, 2015, at 11:02 AM, He-chien Tsai <depo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for reply. I think WAIC is similiar to AIC and BIC.

> They just tell me which one is the best in a collection of models and don't show anything about whether all models in that collection are bad.

Not quite. WAIC provides an approximation of cross-validation
performance. And it does it with the proper posterior instead of
point estimates.

You can use that to compare if you want.
> I'm looking for a method for whether I should accept or reject a model like p-value or significance level. I guess something like that must exists in bayesian approach but I don't know the name.

You can use things like chi-square tests if you insist on trying
to reject a model.

Nothing's going to tell you to accept a model, frequentist or Bayesian.

Models are typically approximations that can always be rejected with
enough data.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to determine goodness of fit?
parts: I don't get this. If that's true, what's p-value actually for?
They’re for confusing poor statistics students.
It also sounds like that every experiment's result by p-value are not confident because every model can always be rejected with enough data.
Yup.  That’s why most practical Bayesians don’t take their models too seriously.

Despite that, I'd like to know what are the most common methods for bayesians to try rejecting a model. Although I found a paper titled "A BAYESIAN χ2 TEST FOR GOODNESS-OF-FIT", I seldom heard this test is used.

Proper Bayesians DO NOT reject models.  Like any hypothesis/significance test,
p-values require that you define both a null hypothesis and a competing hypothesis.
With the competing hypothesis you can compute the power of any testing procedure
which calibrates the resulting p-value.  In a Bayesian setting the null hypothesis is
the full model and there is no competing hypothesis (which would have to be something
like “every other possible model excluding the null” which may not even be expressible
mathematically).  This lack of calibration also effects cross-validation, WAIC, and the
like which is why they can only ever be used for comparisons.

Again, proper Bayesians do not reject models.  Instead we criticize models, looking
for tension with prior beliefs or predictive performance to expand and grow our model.

messages.author: b6fd2925353976cd
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to determine goodness of fit?
parts:
Snarkiness aside, here is what actually happened to me when I presented posterior credible intervals for the parameter of interest (using Stan) in my papers and alongside the interval, I presented p=Prob(b>0) (the posterior probability of the parameter being greater than zero given data), I got the comment, but this is a one-sided significance test; please present the two-tailed test: 1-2*min( P(b<0), P(b>0). 

Since that didn't make any sense at all, I just added the results of the likelihood ratio test based chi-squared using lmer. I think that's a reasonable compromise, because it gives the researcher used to p-values something to look at that they are familiar with at least for making their decision, and at the same time it just presents the amount of information available from the data as a credible interval. Maybe over time the shift will happen, but for now maybe that's good enough. The bottom line seems to be that if I don't want to just stick my results into the proverbial drawer (i.e., "publish papers"), I am going to have to report p-values *alongside* the posterior credible intervals.

If anyone has any better ideas on what to say/do to respond to the criticism that P(b>0) is a one-sided significance test---other than pointing out the obvious fact that it is not---I'm listening.
